2.text: canoe, constructed of three very thin and flexible boards, or dug out of a

3.text: hollow poplar-trunk, while the Chukchee use the skin canoe. The hunters

4.text: occupy a place a little downstream from the trail, and keep very quiet. They

5.text: even refrain from making a fire, in order that the animals may not be frightened

6.text: away by the smell of smoke. The reindeer come to the river, one (usually

7.text: a young active doe) running ahead as leader, and begin to swim across, being

8.text: all the while carried downstream by the current. When the animals are not

9.text: far from the middle of the river, the hunters rush out in canoes and boats,

10.text: and try to impede their progress. The frightened animals turn upstream, and

11.text: exhaust their strength in a vain struggle with the force of the running water;

12.text: then one or two canoes go around the herd in order to cut off their retreat

13.text: to the opposite bank, and slaughtering begins. The reindeer huddle together,

14.text: and float quite helplessly in the middle of the stream. Men in canoes approach

15.text: the herd and stab the reindeer with spears, which have a very long and slender

16.text: shaft, a small iron point, and are not used for any other kind of hunting.

17.text: One side of the double paddle is also often furnished with a small iron spear,

18.text: which, though not so long, is much handier to use (Fig. 47, a).

19.text: The killing is done with incredible rapidity, a man being able to kill as

20.text: many as a hundred animals in one hour. The wound is inflicted on the lower

21.text: part of the body, and the wounded animals immediately turn on the side and

22.text: are carried away by the stream. Most of them do not attempt defence.

23.text: Young strong bucks, however, often try to kick at the canoe, though the

24.text: hunter easily avoids their attack. Those hunters who are most skilful with

25.text: the paddle penetrate into the middle of the herd, and, placing their canoe

26.text: close between two large bucks, spear all the animals within reach, beginning

27.text: with those farthest away; while the nearest, not being disturbed, keep quiet,
27.note: Machine draft read a comma before 'while'; the plate sets a semicolon, confirmed at 2x (zoom crop 27.0).

28.text: and their bodies shield the canoe from the surrounding commotion. Old men,

29.text: women and children, row in boats farther down the river, and intercept the

30.text: game. All animals, when brought to the shore, are skinned. The fattest

31.text: bucks are carved, and some of the meat is hung up to dry. All other car-

32.text: casses are simply deposited in storehouses or in temporary hunting-huts, and

33.text: are used chiefly for dog-food in the winter. A score of Chukchee families

34.text: living in wooden huts on the Middle Anadyr have no herds, and do very

35.text: little fishing, but live exclusively on the produce of the chase; and in a suc-

36.text: cessful season one family will have as their share from a hundred and fifty

37.text: to two hundred reindeer. For their own food they use the animals killed

38.text: late in the season, especially those shot on the ice of the river, because the

39.text: reindeer continue to cross late into the fall, and a few stragglers are met on

40.text: the river even as late as the middle of November.

41.text: The Anui and Omolon Yukaghir, who had only a few dogs, were more

42.text: careful to preserve the meat. They usually cut all the meat in long thin

43.text: strips, drying it on special drying-racks in sun and wind.
